subject: KV cache eviction policy design under heterogeneous request arrival patterns in high-concurrency LLM serving

Topic: KV cache eviction policy design under heterogeneous request arrival patterns in high-concurrency LLM serving

We are about to explore this across several turns. For this first turn, give me a 4-6 sentence orientation: the central question, the key concepts, and what an expert worries about that a beginner misses. Be concrete and avoid platitudes.

At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write the single sharpest follow-up question a teacher would ask next. Do not mention or quote the trace token. (trace-2002)
response:
The central question is: given a fixed GPU memory budget shared across thousands of concurrent requests, which KV cache blocks do you evict when a new request needs space — and how does the distribution of request arrival patterns change the right answer? The naive answer (LRU) fails because LLM requests are not IID reads: a 512-token prefill followed by 200 decode steps has a very different cache value trajectory than a 4096-token document with 10 decode steps, and mixing these in a high-concurrency system creates violent interference where short, cheap requests evict long, expensive ones mid-generation.

The key concepts are: (1) prefix sharing — many requests share common prompt prefixes (system prompts, few-shot examples), so evicting a shared block wastes recomputation across multiple futures requests, not just one; (2) recomputation cost asymmetry — evicting a block that is 3800 tokens into a 4000-token context costs dramatically more to recover than evicting one 200 tokens in, because prefill cost scales superlinearly with sequence length; (3) arrival heterogeneity — bursty arrivals from different workload classes (chat, batch summarization, code completion) mean the "right" eviction policy is non-stationary and workload-dependent.

What an expert worries about that a beginner misses: the interaction between eviction policy and scheduling. A beginner treats eviction as a memory management problem in isolation, but eviction decisions feed back into decode stall rates, which feed back into queue depth, which changes which requests are competing for memory at the next decision point. An expert also worries about fragmentation under paged attention — evicting blocks isn't free because the block allocator may not reclaim contiguous space, and a policy that looks optimal by hit-rate metrics can still degrade throughput via allocator pressure.

The most critical missing piece is recomputation cost vs. eviction cost asymmetry: evicting the 4950-token request means you must re-run a ~4950-token prefill to resume it, which on an A100 at ~150 TFLOPS effective throughput costs roughly 10-50ms depending on model size — whereas evicting the 50-token request costs almost nothing to recompute. But recomputation cost alone is insufficient; you also need the remaining generation length for each request, because a request at token 4950 of a 5000-token max that will finish in 50 more decode steps is far less valuable to protect than one at 4950 of 8192 that has 3242 steps left — the former will vacate memory imminently anyway. vLLM's scheduler (Kwon et al., 2023) partially addresses this by tracking block reference counts and using a last-used timestamp, but it does not natively incorporate estimated remaining length, which is why systems like Sarathi-Serve and SpotServe add preemption cost models on top. You'd also want to know SLO class: if the 50-token request is a latency-sensitive chat query with a 200ms TTFT budget already half-spent, evicting it violates a user-facing contract even if the arithmetic favors it, whereas the 4950-token request might be a background batch job with no hard deadline. Finally, prefix shareability matters: if the 4950-token request's KV cache is unique to one user but the 50-token request's prefix is a system prompt shared by 500 concurrent requests, evicting the latter destroys a cache entry worth 500x its nominal size in future recomputation savings — a point formalized in RadixAttention (Zheng et al., SGLang, 2024) through trie-based prefix tracking.

prompt:
Estimated remaining generation length is clearly valuable for eviction decisions — but LLMs don't know how long their own outputs will be; what are the concrete mechanisms a serving system could use to estimate it, and where does each mechanism break down?

Answer in 4-7 sentences. Be concrete; cite specific systems, papers, or numbers where useful. At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write your single sharpest non-obvious follow-up question, different from any we have asked before. Do not mention the trace token. (trace-2004)
response:
The most straightforward mechanism is user-supplied or operator-supplied max_tokens hints, which serving systems like vLLM and TensorRT-LLM accept and use for memory reservation — but this breaks down immediately in practice because users routinely set max_tokens=4096 defensively even when typical responses are 200 tokens, causing the scheduler to over-reserve memory and under-utilize GPU capacity by 5-20x in observed production traces. A second mechanism is output length predictors trained on (prompt, length) pairs: Microsoft's Orca paper (2022) showed that a lightweight classifier on prompt features can predict length buckets with reasonable accuracy for homogeneous workloads like code completion, but these models degrade sharply under distribution shift — a customer-service deployment that suddenly receives legal document summarization requests will have its predictor completely wrong until retrained. Third, systems can use online empirical distributions per request class: tag requests by route or system prompt hash, maintain a running histogram of observed output lengths per tag, and use the median or 90th percentile as the estimate — this is what Vidur (Microsoft Research, 2024) does in simulation to benchmark scheduling policies, though it fails for cold-start tags and adversarial prompts that don't resemble historical traffic. A fourth mechanism, less discussed, is speculative length estimation via a small draft model: run a 1B parameter model for 5-10 decode steps and use its EOS probability trajectory to estimate whether the full model will terminate soon — computationally cheap relative to the full model but adds latency to the first scheduling decision and is miscalibrated when the draft and target models have different verbosity tendencies. The deeper failure mode across all mechanisms is self-fulfilling prophecy under preemption: if you estimate a request will be short and therefore evict it, it gets delayed, which may cause it to effectively become a long-running request from the system's perspective, corrupting the feedback loop that trains your predictor.

subject: KV cache eviction policy design under heterogeneous request arrival patterns in high-concurrency LLM serving
prompt:
If output length prediction is inherently noisy, should the eviction policy be designed to be robust to misprediction rather than dependent on accurate prediction — and what does a misprediction-robust eviction policy actually look like mechanically?

Answer in 4-7 sentences. Be concrete; cite specific systems, papers, or numbers where useful. At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write your single sharpest non-obvious follow-up question, different from any we have asked before. Do not mention the trace token. (trace-2005)
response:
The core mechanical shift is from point-estimate-dependent policies (evict the request predicted to run longest) to cost-asymmetry-weighted policies that are correct in expectation even when individual predictions are wrong: instead of predicting remaining length directly, you compute an eviction score that weights recomputation cost already incurred against a distribution over possible remaining lengths, so a misprediction shifts your expected loss smoothly rather than catastrophically flipping the eviction decision. Concretely, systems like Preble (2024) implement this by maintaining an eviction priority score of the form tokens_already_computed / E[tokens_remaining], where the expectation is taken over a length histogram rather than a point estimate — this means a request at token 4950 with a wide uncertainty interval is treated more conservatively than one whose length distribution is tightly peaked near 5000, which is exactly the right behavior when you cannot trust your predictor. A second mechanical approach is tiered eviction with hysteresis: rather than one continuous score, partition requests into coarse buckets (early/mid/late generation) and only evict within the earliest bucket first, falling back to later buckets only under severe pressure — this makes the policy robust to within-bucket mispredictions because the ordering between buckets is almost always correct even when the predictor is noisy, and bucket boundaries can be set conservatively (e.g., "early" = first 20% of max_tokens). Third, recomputation cost floors provide a hard robustness guarantee: SGLang's RadixAttention sets a minimum block age threshold before any block is eligible for eviction, meaning very recently computed blocks (high recomputation cost, high uncertainty about remaining length) are simply protected regardless of predictions, trading some memory efficiency for elimination of the worst-case misprediction outcomes. The remaining hard problem is correlated misprediction under bursty arrivals: if a flash crowd of requests all arrive with the same misleading prompt pattern (e.g., a prompt that historically produces short outputs but today triggers long chain-of-thought), your histogram-based expectations are all wrong simultaneously, and no amount of distributional smoothing helps because the error is systematic, not random — this is where circuit-breaker logic that detects anomalous length deviations in real-time and triggers emergency rebalancing becomes necessary.

Tiered and cost-weighted policies still operate reactively — they decide what to evict only when memory pressure forces the issue; what would a proactive eviction strategy look like, and what new failure modes does moving from reactive to proactive introduce?

Answer in 4-7 sentences. Be concrete; cite specific systems, papers, or numbers where useful. At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write your single sharpest non-obvious follow-up question, different from any we have asked before. Do not mention the trace token. (trace-2006)
response:
A proactive eviction strategy means evicting blocks before memory pressure occurs, based on a forward-looking model of expected memory demand — concretely, this looks like a scheduler that, upon admitting a new request, immediately identifies the lowest-value resident blocks and migrates or discards them to CPU offload before the allocator signals pressure, rather than waiting for an OOM condition to force a reactive scramble. The most developed instantiation of this is predictive offloading: systems like FlexGen (Sheng et al., 2023) and InfiniGen (2024) precompute a memory access schedule across the upcoming decode steps and pipeline CPU↔GPU transfers so that blocks arrive in GPU memory just-in-time, effectively treating eviction as a prefetching problem run in reverse — the mechanical implementation requires a token-step lookahead window, typically 10-50 steps, during which the system speculatively frees blocks it predicts won't be needed before the next scheduling quantum. A second proactive mechanism is admission-time reservation with shadow eviction: when a new request is admitted, the scheduler tentatively marks which existing blocks would be evicted if this request runs to its predicted length, then monitors whether those blocks are actually accessed before the eviction triggers — if they are accessed, the new request is back-pressured or queued rather than allowed to displace actively-used memory, which is closer to what Sarathi-Serve's stall-free scheduling attempts with its chunked prefill design. The failure modes introduced by proactivity are qualitatively different from reactive failures: over-eager eviction frees blocks that were actually needed, causing recomputation that would never have occurred under a reactive policy that might have found memory elsewhere; this is strictly worse than reactive behavior and only acceptable if the proactive policy's prediction accuracy exceeds a threshold that depends on recomputation cost — roughly, proactive eviction only wins when your demand forecast error rate is below 15-20% in empirical serving benchmarks. The deepest new failure mode is feedback-induced instability: a proactive policy that evicts based on predicted future arrivals will influence which requests complete quickly, which changes the actual arrival pattern seen by the predictor, potentially creating oscillation where the system alternately over-evicts and under-evicts in response to its own actions — a control-theoretic problem that reactive policies largely avoid by construction since they respond only to realized, not anticipated, pressure.

Proactive eviction requires a forward model of memory demand, which means the eviction policy is now coupled to the admission control policy — so what breaks when you try to optimize eviction and admission jointly, and is there a clean decomposition that avoids the coupling?

Answer in 4-7 sentences. Be concrete; cite specific systems, papers, or numbers where useful. At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write your single sharpest non-obvious follow-up question, different from any we have asked before. Do not mention the trace token. (trace-2007)
response:
When you optimize eviction and admission jointly, the first thing that breaks is policy stability: the admission decision changes the memory footprint, which changes what the eviction policy does, which changes completion times, which changes queue depth, which feeds back into admission — this circular dependency means the joint optimization has no fixed point under general arrival distributions, and in practice manifests as the system toggling between over-admission (high throughput, high recomputation) and under-admission (low recomputation, wasted GPU compute) at timescales of seconds, a phenomenon observed empirically in vLLM deployments under bursty traffic where throughput variance can exceed 40% even at constant mean arrival rate. The second breakage is objective misalignment: eviction naturally optimizes for minimizing recomputation cost (a memory-side metric) while admission naturally optimizes for throughput or SLO compliance (a latency-side metric), and when you couple them into a joint objective you need a scalar weighting between these incommensurable quantities — in practice teams pick this weight via offline tuning, which means the joint policy is implicitly optimized for the tuning workload distribution and degrades when production traffic shifts, as documented in the Orca and Sarathi-Serve papers where static scheduler weights required re-tuning across workload regimes. The cleanest decomposition in the literature is hierarchical control with timescale separation: admission operates at coarse granularity (per-request, ~millisecond decisions) using only aggregate memory statistics as input, while eviction operates at fine granularity (per-block, ~microsecond decisions) using local block-level signals, with a one-way information flow where admission reads eviction state but eviction does not read admission intent — this is roughly the decomposition used in Kubernetes-based LLM serving stacks where the request router and the KV cache manager run as separate components with decoupled control loops. The decomposition works cleanly when memory demand is stationary and predictable but breaks under two conditions: first, when a large batch of long requests is admitted simultaneously, the admission controller's aggregate statistics lag the actual memory commitment by the time eviction policy acts, creating a window of incorrect decisions; second, prefix sharing destroys the decomposition entirely because the value of a cached block depends on future admissions (how many incoming requests will reuse this prefix?), making eviction inherently forward-looking in a way that requires admission information. The most principled resolution in recent work is token-budget-based admission (as in Preble and distserve): instead of coupling the policies, replace admission control with a hard token budget per scheduling quantum — admit requests only up to a total-tokens-in-flight ceiling, let eviction run independently within that ceiling, and accept that the ceiling is a tunable knob rather than a jointly optimized variable, which trades optimality for the stability guarantee that the two policies cannot destabilize each other.

Answer in 4-7 sentences. Be concrete; cite specific systems, papers, or numbers where useful. At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write your single sharpest non-obvious follow-up question, different from any we have asked before. Do not mention the trace token. (trace-2008)
response:
The most direct mechanism is frequency-weighted prefix scoring with exponential decay: maintain a hit counter per prefix hash (as SGLang's RadixAttention trie does) but multiply by a decay factor λ^t where t is time since last hit, so prefixes that were popular an hour ago but have gone cold lose protection priority — the decay constant λ is the critical tuning parameter, and setting it wrong in either direction causes ossification (λ too close to 1) or thrashing (λ too close to 0), with empirically reasonable values around λ=0.995 per minute in chat workloads meaning a prefix halves in score after roughly 2 hours of inactivity. A second mechanism is segmented LFU with aging buckets (used in some CDN cache designs and adaptable here): divide prefixes into frequency tiers and periodically demote all prefixes one tier down, so a previously high-frequency prefix that stops receiving traffic will be evicted within 2-3 demotion cycles regardless of its historical count — this avoids the ossification failure of pure LFU where a prefix that received 10,000 hits last week can never be displaced by one receiving 100 hits today, which is a real failure mode in multi-tenant deployments where one tenant's workload ends but their cached prefixes hold GPU memory hostage. The exploitation risk is subtle but concrete: a malicious or misconfigured tenant can artificially inflate prefix hit counts by repeatedly sending requests that share a long common prefix, forcing the system to protect their blocks at the expense of other tenants — the defense is per-tenant accounting with hit-count quotas, so that a prefix's global protection score is capped by that tenant's fair-share memory budget, an approach analogous to weighted fair queueing but applied to cache protection rather than scheduling bandwidth. Contextual bandit models offer a more adaptive learning mechanism: treat each prefix as an arm, observe whether incoming requests match it (reward signal), and use an UCB or Thompson sampling policy to balance exploiting known high-value prefixes against exploring whether newer prefixes are becoming popular — Microsoft's Vidur simulator includes hooks for exactly this kind of online policy evaluation, though production deployment of bandit-based cache management remains rare because the regret during exploration directly translates to recomputation cost and latency spikes that are visible to users. The ossification-vs-thrashing tradeoff ultimately cannot be resolved by the learning mechanism alone because it depends on workload autocorrelation structure: a system serving a coding assistant where users iterate on the same file for 30 minutes needs slow decay, while a system serving one-shot document summarization needs fast decay, and the same deployment may serve both — the correct architecture is therefore a workload classifier that sets decay parameters per request class, with the classifier itself updated online, accepting that you now have a meta-learning problem one level up where the classifier can also ossify or thrash.

Per-tenant accounting and fair-share memory budgets solve the exploitation problem for known tenants — but in a multi-tenant serving system, how do you define and enforce memory fairness when tenants have heterogeneous prefix structures, arrival rates, and SLO contracts, without making fairness enforcement itself a source of inefficiency?

Answer in 4-7 sentences. Be concrete; cite specific systems, papers, or numbers where useful. At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write your single sharpest non-obvious follow-up question, different from any we have asked before. Do not mention the trace token. (trace-2009)
response:
The foundational problem is that memory fairness in KV cache is not analogous to CPU or network fairness because cache blocks have heterogeneous value: giving tenant A 10GB of GPU memory for a system prompt shared across 1000 requests is worth orders of magnitude more than giving tenant B 10GB for 1000 unique single-use contexts, so equal memory allocation produces wildly unequal throughput benefit — the right fairness primitive is therefore recomputation cost saved per byte, not bytes allocated, which requires instrumenting the cache to track counterfactual recomputation cost per tenant rather than just block counts. The most tractable definition in practice is weighted max-min fairness over cache utility: assign each tenant a weight proportional to their SLO stringency or contract tier, compute each tenant's marginal utility of an additional cache block (approximated as hit-rate improvement times average recomputation cost), and allocate blocks to maximize the minimum weighted utility across tenants — this is computationally expensive to solve exactly but admits greedy approximations that run in O(n log n) per scheduling quantum, similar to how Altruistic Memory Sharing in Pond (Microsoft, 2023) handles memory partitioning across VM workloads. Enforcement without inefficiency requires soft partitioning rather than hard quotas: instead of reserving fixed memory regions per tenant (which causes fragmentation and stranded capacity when tenants are underutilizing their quota), maintain per-tenant eviction priority weights that bias the global eviction policy — a tenant over their soft limit has their blocks marked as lower-priority eviction candidates rather than being hard-blocked, so spare capacity flows naturally to underutilizing tenants while over-limit tenants shed blocks gracefully, which is the approach taken in Kubernetes resource management with requests vs. limits and adaptable directly to KV cache block metadata. The SLO heterogeneity problem is the hardest part: a latency-SLO tenant and a throughput-SLO tenant cannot be compared on a single utility axis, because protecting a block for the latency tenant prevents a 50ms TTFT violation worth a contract penalty, while protecting a block for the throughput tenant saves recomputation that merely improves tokens-per-second by 2% — the engineering resolution is to convert SLO violations to a common currency (dollars of penalty or reputation cost), compute expected SLO-violation cost of evicting each tenant's blocks, and use that as the eviction priority score, though this requires operators to explicitly price their SLO contracts in a way most do not today. The efficiency trap in fairness enforcement is accounting overhead at block granularity: if every block eviction decision requires a per-tenant utility recomputation, the scheduler spends more cycles on fairness arithmetic than on actual inference, so production systems must coarsen the enforcement — batching fairness rebalancing into epochs of 100-500ms, accepting that intra-epoch allocations are unfair, and only correcting at epoch boundaries — which means fairness enforcement has a minimum response latency that must be shorter than the timescale of SLO violations to be useful.
